title: Ordinary local henselization agrees with maximal-ideal pair henselization
statement: Let $(A,\mathfrak m)$ be a commutative local ring. Let $(K,J)$, with structure map $\eta:A\to K$, be the henselization of the pair $(A,\mathfrak m)$ [lem-weil-pbc-pair-henselization]. Then $K$ is local henselian [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology], its maximal ideal is $J=\mathfrak mK$, and $\eta$ is local and induces an isomorphism $A/\mathfrak m\xrightarrow{\sim}K/J$. Moreover $K$ is an ordinary henselization of $A$: for every henselian local ring $S$ and every local map $A\to S$ there is a unique local $A$-algebra map $K\to S$. Consequently the ordinary henselization $A^h$ [def-weil-pbc-henselization-at-prime] is canonically isomorphic to $K$ as a local $A$-algebra.

source.place: Tag 0A03, lemma-henselization-local-ring, statement and proof, including the maximal-ideal and residue identifications.

proof.text: Apply [lem-weil-pbc-pair-henselization] to $(A,\mathfrak m)$. For its colimit $K$ and structure map $\eta$, we have $J=\mathfrak mK$, the pair $(K,J)$ is henselian, and the canonical map $e:A/\mathfrak m\xrightarrow{\sim}K/J$ is an isomorphism. In particular $K/J$ is a nonzero field, so $J$ is proper and maximal: ideals containing $J$ correspond to ideals of the field $K/J$, which are zero and the whole field.

source.place: Tag 0A03, lemma-henselization-local-ring, opening paragraph; Tag 0A02, lemma-henselization, quotient calculation.

proof.text: For $z\in J$, consider the cyclic, hence finite, $K$-algebra $D=K/(1-z)$. In $D$ the image of $z$ is $1$, so $JD=D$ and $D/JD$ is the zero ring. By the idempotent-lifting definition [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology], its single idempotent has a unique idempotent lift to $D$. Both $0_D$ and $1_D$ lift it; hence $0_D=1_D$. Thus $(1-z)=K$ and $1-z$ is a unit of $K$. This directly supplies the radical consequence needed in the opening paragraph of Stacks 0A03.

source.place: Tag 0A03, lemma-henselization-local-ring, radical argument; Tag 09XI, lemma-characterize-henselian-pair, idempotent-lifting criterion.

proof.text: If $x\notin J$, choose $y\in K$ whose residue is the inverse of $x+J$ in $K/J$. Then $1-xy\in J$, so Step 2 makes $xy$ a unit, and $x$ is a unit (if $vxy=1$, then $vy$ is its inverse). No element of $J$ is a unit since $J$ is proper. Thus the nonunits are exactly $J$ and every proper ideal is contained in $J$: $K$ is local with maximal ideal $J$. Since $(K,J)$ is henselian, $K$ is henselian local by [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology]. Finally $\eta(a)\in J$ if and only if $e(a+\mathfrak m)=0$, if and only if $a\in\mathfrak m$. Hence $\eta$ is local and its residue-field map is precisely $e$.

source.place: Tag 0A03, lemma-henselization-local-ring, opening paragraph, with the unit and contraction arguments written out.

proof.text: Let $S$ be henselian local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak n$, and let $g:A\to S$ be local. By [def-weil-pbc-henselian-terminology], $(S,\mathfrak n)$ is a henselian pair, and locality gives $g(\mathfrak m)\subseteq\mathfrak n$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-henselization-universal-property] with $(B,J)=(A,\mathfrak m)$, $(A',I')=(S,\mathfrak n)$ and $\varphi=g$. It gives a unique ring map $h:K\to S$ with $h\eta=g$ and $h(J)\subseteq\mathfrak n$. If $x\notin J$, Step 3 makes $x$ a unit, so $h(x)$ is a unit and is outside $\mathfrak n$. Thus $h^{-1}(\mathfrak n)=J$ and $h$ is local. Every local $A$-algebra map extending $g$ is a ring-map extension, so the same uniqueness gives the asserted unique local extension.

source.place: Tag 0A02, lemma-henselization, final paragraph (adjunction), applied after the locality proved in Tag 0A03.

proof.text: Since $A$ is local, its localization $A_{\mathfrak m}$ is canonically $A$: each denominator outside $\mathfrak m$ is already a unit and $a/s\mapsto as^{-1}$ is inverse to the localization map. Accordingly [def-weil-pbc-henselization-at-prime] identifies the universal property of Step 4 with ordinary henselization. For any chosen ordinary henselization $\eta_H:A\to H=A^h$, Step 4 gives a unique local $A$-map $u:K\to H$; the defining property of $H$ gives a unique local $A$-map $v:H\to K$. The local composites $vu$ and $\mathrm{id}_K$ both extend $\eta$, so Step 4 gives $vu=\mathrm{id}_K$. The defining uniqueness for $H$ gives $uv=\mathrm{id}_H$. These inverse maps give the canonical local $A$-algebra isomorphism $A^h\cong K$; uniqueness also proves independence of the chosen representatives.
